DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, from 1st April, 2002 the

followed now for fixing petroleum prices after the dismantling of the 
administered pricing system. 
SHRI RAM NAIK: The oil companies look into the international prices and 
take their decisions, but when the prices become very volatile, we also try to 
see if we can help the consumers so that they are insulated from very high 
price-increase.

June, we reduced the excise duty thereby reducing the burden. So far as

consumers are a little insulated from the heavy prices in international market.

Dam on river flowing from Nepal 
†*282. PROF. RAM DEO BHANDARY: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the progress made in the discussion between India and 
Nelpal for constructing dams over rivers passing through Bihar and originating 
from Nepal; 
(b) whether representative of Bihar Government is included in the 
discussion; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to solve the problem of the 
floods in Bihar due to these rivers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) In pursuance to the decision taken by the Hon'ble Prime Minister of 
Nepal and India during July-August, 2000, the India-Nepal Joint Committee 
on Water Resources (JCWR) was set up to discuss all important issues 
between India and Nepal on water resources including storage schemes to 
control floods in rivers flowing from Nepal namely, Sapta Kosi High Dam 
Multipurpose Project & Sun Kosi Storage cum Diversion Scheme on river 
Kosi, Kamla Multipurpose Project on river Kamla and Bagmati Multipurpose 
Project on river Bagmati. 
In respect of Sapta Kosi High Dam Multipurpose Project & Sun Kosi 
Storage cum Diversion Scheme, the Joint Team of Experts (JTE) of India-
Nepal has already come to an understanding and an Inception Report of this 
project has been finalised to be a guiding document for the Joint Study Team 
for preparation of the Detailed Project Report (DPR). The Government of 
India has already approved the proposal for setting up of a Joint Project 
Office to take up the Joint field investigation/studies and preparation of DPR 
for the Project. 
Proposal for construction of Multipurpose Storage dams on river Kamla 
near Chisapani and on river Bagmati near Noonthar in Nepal

are under discussion with Nepal. Efforts to work out an understanding in this 
regard are in progress though Nepalese feel that these projects may not be 
feasible because of social and environmental implications. 
(b) Yes, Sir. The Engineer-in-Chief (Water Resources Department), 
Government of Bihar is representing the State Government in the Joint Team 
of Experts. 
(c) Flood Management being a State subject, the responsibility of 
planning, funding, executing and operating flood control schemes rests with 
the concerned State Government. The assistance rendered by the Central 
Government is technical, catalytic and promotional in nature. 
Ganga Flood Control Commission under the Ministry of Water 
Resources has prepared comprehensive plans for flood management for all the 
rivers causing floods in the Ganga basin and sent the same to the State 
Governments including Bihar for implementation of the recommendation 
made therein. In addition, the Government of India has also set up a number 
of Committees/Expert Groups to study the problem of floods, the 
recommendations of which have been sent to the State Governments 
including Bihar for implementation. 
The Central Government has also been providing financial assistance to 
the State Government through various Centrally Sponsored Scheme to take 
up the works under critical anti-erosion schemes, raising & strengthening and 
extension of embankments along the rivers; and flood proofing programme 
such as construction of raised platforms and drainage channels. In addition, as 
a non-structural measure to forewarn and manage flood disasters, a plan 
scheme namely, "Flood Forecasting & Warning system on rivers common to 
India & Nepal" has also been in operation since 1989.

Master Plan for Rain Water Harvesting 
*285.   SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD:†† 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Central Ground Water Board has formulated a Rs. 
24,500 crore master plan for harvesting rain in the entire country to solve 
country's worsening water crisis; 
(b) if so, what are the main features of this proposal; 
(c) what is the total amount to be spent for implementing this project; 
and 
(d) by when the work on this project is likely to start and by when it is 
likely to be completed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (d) A 
statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
 
Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) has prepared a report entitled 
"Master Plan for Artificial Recharge to Groundwater", which envisages 
recharge of 36453 Million Cubic Metre Volume of surplus monsoon runoff 
through construction of 39.25 lakh artificial recharge and rooftop rainwater 
harvesting structures.The report outlines broad framework about feasibility of 
these recharge structures in various parts of the country. 
The details of funding pattern, implementing agencies, etc. are under 
discussion. In view of this, the schedule for its implementation cannot be 
indicated at this stage. 
SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Sir, While I appreciate the decision 
taken by the Government of India to construct 39.25 lakh artificial rooftop 
rainwater   harvesting   structures,   I   would   like  to   ask  the 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Gulam Nabi Azad. 
22 

[11 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
hon. Minister by when funding pattern and implementing agencies will be 
finalised. I would also like to know whether the Government has sought the 
involvement of non-governmental and voluntary organisations for harvestinng 
rainwater. If so, to what extent, their involvement has been useful. Part (b) of 
my question is, whether the Government is making any effort to develop new 
technology in addition to the conventional methods of conserving rainwater in 
urban areas as well as rural areas. 
SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY: Sir, I am very grateful to the 
hon. Member because it is a very appropriate question. In fact, the ground water 
level in the country is on the decline. It is because of the population pressure, 
industrial and agricultural activities. Because of all these reasons, in the last 20 
years, there has been a decline of four metres in the ground water level in some 
areas. That is why the Ministry of Water Resources has taken recourse to 
rainwater harvesting measure.The hon. Member has also asked about the 
proposal. Sir, it is simply a blueprint and it is a vision of the Ministry. Because 
if the ground water level goes down in this way, then, in the course of time, by 
2025 or 2030, there will be no water at all in the country. As regards the second part 
of the question, although we earmark a large amount of money, but, actually, it 
will be completed within a span of ten years. We want to involve people from the 
ground level to the upper level—from the Water User Associations to the gram 
panchayat level, then, to the district level and, then, to the State level, In this 
way, we want to involve all the people so that they can understand the 
necessity of sustainability of the ground water. And if we do not sustain water 
now, it is expected that there will be great scarcity of water in the near future. 
On the question whether we should develop a modern technology or not, I 
would like to say that, certainly, we are experimenting on it. We have already 
made some experiments in this regard and we have been successful in Gujarat, 
Rajasthan and in Delhi itself. Basically, we have attempted to construct 
structures more in the urban areas than in the rural areas. But, in the course of 
time, we will surely shift there. 
SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Sir, as the hon. Minister said, we all 
know that the ground water level is on the decline. With the increase in 
population, and sometimes, on account of the monsoon failure, it has been 
observed that special measures have to be taken to increase the renewable 
water resources, in all possible ways. May I ask the 
23 

RAJYA  SABHA [11 March, 2003] 
hon. Minister whether the Government is thinking of educating and involving 
the whole nation in this most important and most needed aspect of water 
conservation by introducing this as a separate subject in the curriculum? I still 
remember that my teacher—when I was in primary class—used to say that if 
you find a water tap running, put it off; If you find a bulb glowing 
unnecessarily, put it off. That is why, when I went to Japan and America, I 
would put off the tap. So, if we are educated right from the beginning, from 
the childhood, I think, it will have a great effect. There is also a need for 
aggressive electronic and media campaign in this regard. Is something being 
done in this direction? 
SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY: We have already taken 
measures in this regard. We have already started awareness campaign 
throughout the country. We have already covered many districts of the 
country and we have started fresh water year which has been declared as such 
by the UNO. The Ministry of Water Resources already has some programmes 
to involve the school and college students also. We want to involve NGOs 
also in this regard. We have got a vast country; we have got a diverse 
topographical and geographical area. In some parts of the country, there is 
heavy rainfall and in some parts of the country, there is scanty rainfall. So, all 
these things place us in a very peculiar situation. Sir, that is why we feel that 
we have to save each drop of water, which is very valuable and valuable than 
any kind of valuable material. 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, in the background of

of Water Resources require Rs.24,000 crores for Master Plan. I would like to 
know from the hon. Minister whether it is difficult to mobilise so much 
money in the Tenth plan. Are you planning to provide some money from the 
Rural Development Ministry out of the Tenth Plan? Would you make efforts 
to makes it useful for the States like Rajasthan and other States so that this 
scheme is made successful? 
24 

[11 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY: It is a very important question put

Tax on companies incorporated in Mauritius 
*290. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it has been decided to tax companies incorporated in 
Mauritius if such companies have their place of effective management in 
India; 
38 

[11 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) since when the decision is going to take effect? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) and (b) Companies incorporated in Mauritius and having 
their place of effective management in India are laible to tax in India under the 
Double Taxation Avoidance Convention (DTAC) bet\ India and Mauritius. 
Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) had ea; issued a Circular No. 789 dated 
13.4.2000 to clarify provisions regarding taxation of income from dividends 
and Capital Gains under the Indo-Maurities DTAC. This Circular also specified 
that the certificate of residence issued by the Mauritian authorities should be 
regarded as sufficient proof of residence of an entity in Mauritius. To remove 
any doubts regarding the effect of Circular No. 789 dated 13.4.2000, CBDT 
issued another Circular, No. 1/2003 dated 10.2.2003, wherein it has been 
clarified that where it is found as a fact that a company has its place of 
effective management in India, then notwithstanding its being incorporated in 
Mauritius, it would be taxed in India as per Indo-Mauritius DTAC. 
(c) The Circular No. 1 /2003 dated 10th February, 2003 merely clarifies the 
provisions of Indo-Mauritius DTAC which is effective in India from 1 st April, 
1983.

Captain Dastur was examined by two committees of Experts comprising experts 
from Central Water Commission, State Governments and Professors from 
Indian Institute of Technology and University of Roorkee who were of the 
opinion that the proposal was technically unsound and economically prohibitive. 
Similarly, the Ganga-Gauvery link was examined by Central Water 
Commission and found to be grossly under estimated. Besides, the proposal 
was also devoid of any flood control benefit and required large block of power 
for lifting water. Both proposals were, therefore, given up. 
(e) to (g) The feasibility studies being carried out by National Water 
Development Agency cover studies pertaining to environment and ecological 
surveys. In its studies, a minimum lean season flow of 10% of the total flows at 
diversion structure after meeting downstream requirements is being provided 
to maintain the environmental and ecological needs of the river regime and the 
downstream areas including coastal water and fisheries resources.

Compulsory Demat 
2043. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the reasons for making demat compulsory when it is optional even in 
countries like the US; 
(b) whether small investor has been adversely hit by the fixed charges by 
National Security Depository Ltd. (NSDL); 
(c) what has been the impact of compulsory demat on the growth of the 
capital market; and 
(d) whether Government have any proposal to review the working of the 
NSDL? 
82 

[11 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) The 
Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has not made 
dematerialisation compulsory for any investor. Under the Depositories Act, 
1996 investors can choose holding of securities either in physical or in demat 
form. 
SEBI has however made all trading and settlement of securities on Stock 
Exchanges compulsory in demat form. This has been done to protect the 
interest of investors from all the problems associated with physical securities 
such as bad deliveries, fake, forged and stolen securities. 
However, the Stock Exchange have the facility by which investors can 
sell upto 500 shares in physical form on the Stock Exchanges. 
(b) Depositories are organisations which are expected to run on 
commercial basis and provide a service to the investors and the market 
participants at a cost. Over a period of time, the depository charges 
have reduced due to competition. 
The tariff revision that came into force from May 2002 has two new 
components of charges; 
(1) Fixed charges on transactions replacing the old sytem of 
charging on the basis of ad-valorem. 
(2) Custody charges on the basis of holding the securities of number 
of companies on monthly basis. 
NSDL has brought in both of the above mentioned new charges. The 
tariff changes by the depositories is a commercial issue. The total number of 
demat accounts have increased from 37.02 lakh accounts in April 2002 to the 
present around 38.19 lakh accounts (as on February 2003). In the last one year, 
demat stock has grown from Rs. 4728 crore to Rs. 6045 crore. This continuous 
growth of dematerialisation is indicative of the cost-effectiveness of the system. 
(c) Depositories and dematerialisation had a very positive impact on 
the growth of the capital market. It has eliminated problems associated 
with bad paper, elminated problems related to transfer fo shares (transfer 
of shares in now instantaneous) and has helped reduce the settlement 
83 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2003] 
period thereby paving the way for rolling settlement. It has also helped in 
removing the market lot concept, splitting and consolidating of shares besides 
reducing the risks and transaction cost, thereby increasing the efficiency of the 
market. 
(d) In view of the representations received from investors about the 
adverse effects of new tariff of depositories, SEBI has constituted an internal 
Committee viz. "Demat Cost Committee" to examine whether the new tariff is 
justifiable from view point of small investors.

home loan interest or provide some subsidy to facilitate middle and lower 
rank employees of organised sector to purchase houses; 
(e) if so, the details thereof; and 
(f) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. In the monetary policy statement announced by RBI on April 29, 2002, 
RBI recognized the growing importance of the construction sector including its 
forward and backward linkages with other sectors of the economy and 
encouraged banks to increase the flow of credit to this sector. 
With a view to further improve the flow of credit to housing sector, in the 
recenlty announced Monetary & Credit Policy for the year 2002-03 RBI 
proposed to liberalise the prudential requirements for housing finance by banks 
and encourage investment by banks in securitised debt instruments of 
Housing Finance Companies (HFCs), Accordingly: 
The term loans extended by bankis to intermediary agencies against the 
loans sanctioned by them have been allowed to be reckoned as part of 
housing finance. Also, investment in bonds issued by HUDCO and 
NHB exclusively for financing of housing is being reckoned for 
priority sector targets. 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2003] 
Banks extending loans against residential housing properties would be 
required to assign risk weight of 50 percent, instead of present 100 
percent. 
Investments made by banks in Mortgage Backed Securities (MBS) of 
residential assets by HFCs, which are recognized and supervised by 
NHB, would also be assigned a risk weight of 50 percent for the 
purpose of capital adequacy. 
Investments by banks in MBS issued by HFCs supervised by NHB 
will be reckoned for inclusion in the prescribed housing finance 
allocation of 3.0 percent. 
Commercial banks have been given freedom to decide their lending rates 
for credit limits over Rs. 2 lakh since October 1994. In April 2001 Monetary 
and Credit Policy, PLR was converted into a reference or benchmark rate so 
that banks are now free to lend at a sub-PLR rate to creditworthy borrowers 
including public enterprises on the lines of a transparent and objective policy 
approved by their Boards. Therefore, banks have the flexibility to reduce rate 
on home loans under the extant guidelines en lending rates. The lending rates 
of commercial banks have generally responded to the comfortable liquidity 
situation. As many as 21 public sector banks, 14 private banks and 6 foreign 
banks reduced their PLRs since the announcement of midterm review in 
October 2002. While the reduction in PLR by public sector banks was to the 
tune of 50 to 100 basis points, the same for private banks ranged from 50 to 
200 basis points and for foreign banks it was 25 to 325 basis points.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) Yes, 
Sir. Securities and Exchange Board of India (Delisting of Securities) 
Guidelines 2003, have been issued on February 17, 2003 with the objective 
of protecting and interest of investors in the securities market. 
(b) to (d) Important provisions in the guidelines are: 
(i) In addition to voluntary and compulsory delisting, Guidelines shall be 
applicable to any acquisition of shares of the company (either by a 
promoter or by any other person) or scheme or arrangement, by whatever 
name referred to, consequent to which the public shareholding falls 
below the minimum limit specified in the listing conditions or listing 
agreement that may result In delisting of securities. 
(ii) Company shall not be permitted to use the buy-back provision to delist 
its securities. 
(iii) Companies can delist from stock exchanges only by offering an exit 
route to remaining shareholders through a reverse book building 
process. This mechanism would allow shareholders to bid to sell on 
the screen of any stock exchange with nation wide access and the 
highest price at which the maximum number of shareholders would 
be willing to sell would be the offer price. Further, the promoter shall 
offer a floor price on the basis of average of previous 26-week's high 
and low prices to investors. 
(iv) If the quantity eligible for acquiring securities at the final price offered 
does not result in public shareholding falling below required level of 
public holding for continuous listing, the company shall remain listed. 
(v) Stock exchanges may, in addition to present cases of compulsory 
delisting, delist companies which have been suspended for a minimum 
period of six months for non-compliance with the Listing Agreement. 
These guidelines seek to protect the interests of the small investors in the 
wake of any company delisting from the exchanges.

Achievements of economic reforms 
2970. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed and analysed the achievement of 
economic reforms in tackling the poverty and raising the standard of living of 
poor and lower middle class people in this country; 
(b) if so, Government's assessment thereof; 
115 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2003] 
(c) whether it is also a fact that economic reforms have failed to increase 
GDP at the desired level; 
(d) if so, whether it is due to improper implementation of the policies 
under economic reforms or otherwise; and 
(e) the steps being taken to ensure that the benefits of economic reforms 
reach poor and common man? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) to (e) 
Economic Reforms are a continuous process and these reforms are reviewed 
from time to time based on the prevailing situation. 
Various economic reforms measures have been taken by the Government 
since 1991 aimed at accelerating economic growth, facilitating greater 
investment, enhancing the competitive spirit, reducing the level of poverty, 
allowing higher private initiative and achieving greater integration with the 
world economy. The reforms have resulted in improved growth of the 
economy, a lower rate of inflation, an overall increase in flows of foreign 
direct investment, a significant improvement in the balance of payments 
position, accumulation of comfortable foreign exchange reserves and an all 
round improvement in the external debt indicators.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. Though the uptrend in global oil prices have caused some 
inflationary undercurrents, pushing up the annual point to point inflation rate 
based on the Wholesale Price Index to 4.9 percent in mid February 2003, there 
is not much cause for worry, as stability in the prices of primary and 
manufactured products would help keep inflation under control despite the rise in 
fuel prices. 
Government is making concerted efforts to keep inflation under control 
through effective supply management as also through close monitoring of 
prices and supply of essential commodities. Large volumes of public stock of 
foodgrains have ensured comfortable supply situation

Effect of rise in prices of petrol and diesel 
2074. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN "DURRU": Will the Minister 
of FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the impact on inflation due to periodic increase in the prices of petrol 
and diesel; 
(b) whether the regular inflationary trend is a matter of great concern to the 
common people of the country; and 
(c) what action Government propose to take to contain the inflation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) 
With the dismantling of the Administered Price Mechanism from April 1, 2002, 
domestic diesel and petrol prices are market determined and linked to the 
movement of international crude oil prices. The transition from an administered 
to a market based pricing regime has been quite smooth so far. The annual point 
to point inflation rate based on the WPI remained below 2 per cent till the end 
of May 2002, and rose thereafter only to remain between 3-4 per cent level 
during much of the current financial year. The uptrend in global oil prices 
caused some inflationary undercurrents towards mid January 2003 pushing up 
the inflation rate to over 4% level for the first time in 2002-03. The latest annual 
point to point inflation rate for the week ended February 15,2003 is 4.9 percent, 
which is still quite moderate. Stability in the prices of primary and manufactured 
products would help keep inflation under control, thus preventing any undue 
harships to the common people of the country. 
(c) Government is making concerted efforts to keep inflation under 
control through effective supply management as also through close 
monitoring of prices and supply of essential commodities. Large volumes of 
public stock of foodgrains have ensured comfortable supply situation of 
foodgrains and helped stabilise their prices despite the severity of drought. 
Government's liberal release of surplus foodgrain stocks under various 
welfare schemes has provided increased support to the vulnerable sections of 
the society.

Interest rate differentials between US and India 
2089. SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Non-Resident Indians are depositing their 
money to seize opportunity presented by the interest rate differentials 
between the US and India; 
(b) if so, its impact on the Indian economy; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to reduce the interest rate difference 
between the two countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) to (c) A 
recent study by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on "Accretion to Foreign 
Exchange Reserve in India : Sources, Arbitrage and Costs", indicates that non-
resident Indian (NRI) deposits have experienced a net increase of US $2.1 billion 
during April-November 2002, compared with an almost identical increase of 
US $2.2 billion during April-November 2001. The accretion includes 
drawdown of deposits from the non-resident, non-convertible rupee accounts, 
which were discontinued from March 2002. Since 1999-2000, annual net inflows 
in NRI deposits have ranged between US$1.5-2.7 billion.Thus, the current trends 
in non-resident deposits have been consistent with those observed during the past 
few years. The RBI study points out that despite a differential of 3-4 percent 
between Indian and international interest rates, there is no evidence to suggest 
that arbitrage opportunities have led to accretion of foreign exchange reserves in 
India. It is also mentionable that over the years there has been a downward 
trend in Indian interest rates facilitated by moderate inflation and adequate 
liquidity in the economy.

Need for a statement from the Prime Minister on the latest situation on Iraq 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Madam, with your  
permission, I would like to draw the attention of the House to an important 
matter. Yesterday, we drew the attention of the Government to the statement 
of the Prime Minister on the situation in Iraq. Since the Budget session of the 
Parliament began, the Prime Minister did not make any statement on the 
situation developing in Iraq, except making some cursory references while 
replying to the Motion of Thanks on the President's Address. On the whole 
issue, the country has not learnt anything from the Prime Minister through the 
floor of the House. To my mind, Madam, this is an unusual situation. We do 
appreciate that the Prime Minister invites the leaders of the opposition parties 
and shares his concern with them. We fully appreciate it. At the same time, we 
do expect that the Prime Minister would take this House and the other House 
into confidence and explain the position of the Government, express the 
concern of one hundred crores of people whom he is representing because 
this is a matter on which each and every one of us is concerned, not only 
because a large number of people are staying there but also because of the 
very fact that just a 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2003] 
decade ago, when the Gulf crisis arose, what a terrible price the country had 
to pay in terms of balance of payments. Our foreign exchange reserves came 
down to just a month's requirement. According to some statistics, if the war 
continues for more than two weeks, the oil prices may go up to $36 to $40 per 
barrel. 
Keeping all these objectives in view, we requested for a statement by 
the Prime Minister. I was glad - I do not know whether I had the wrong 
impression - that the hon. Minister of Parliamentary Affairs intervened and 
pointed out that it is not correct that the Prime Minister will not make any 
statement. Yesterday, she pointed out that the Prime Minister was meeting the 
leaders of the opposition parties and after that he will come and make a 
statement on the floor of this House. If the Government wants to retract its 
position from there, the Government is entitled to do so. But when the Minister 
of Parliamentary Affairs gives some sort of assurance - at least, I took it as 
assurance from the hon. Minister of Parliamentary Affairs -- I think, the whole 
Government is giving that assurance, because this House communicates either 
through the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs, or, through the Leader of the 
House. Therefore, in the fitness of the things, if the Government finds that they 
will not make any statement, it should have been proper on the part of the 
Government to inform the House that the Government is not going to make 
any statement. We read in the newspaper that the Prime Minister had 
conversation and discussion with the American President, George Bush and 
the House has no right to know that from the Prime Minister. 
It is true that we debated and discussed the whole issue on a Private 
Members' Resolution on last Friday. The hon. Minister of External Affairs 
responded to the debate and there is no doubt that many of my colleagues 
have expressed their satisfaction on the way he responded to the issue. But, 
apart from that, is it not incumbent on the Prime Minister -who is the leader of 
the nation, who is the leader of the country - to take both the Houses into 
confidence and share his concern, express his views and the decision? 
Madam, on this matter, there is a broad unanimity as I remember, 
when I raised this issue, even some of the supporters of the ruling party -Mr. 
Virumbi and some others - joined me in expressing the concern. Therefore,  
most respectfully,  I would like to submit, through you, to the 
204 

[11 March, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Government to let the Prime Minister come and make a statement. The 
country expects that on this occasion the Prime Minister would rise and fulfil 
the expectations and aspirations of the people of the country. What they are 
saying in the United Nations, we appreciate that. What the Minister of External 
Affairs replied to the Private Members' Resolution, we appreciate that also. 
But that is not a substitute of the Prime Minister taking the House into 
confidence. The All-Party meeting is no substitute of taking the Parliament into 
confidence and the Prime Minister making a statement on the floor of this 
House. Therefore, most respectfully, I would like to submit, through you, that 
the Government should ensure the Prime Minister comes and makes a 
statement. There may be many sensitive issues that will come up like whether 
we will allow the airplanes, the warplanes to be fuelled on the Indian soil, 
whether the Indian soil will be used or not -- all these issues will come up 
when the war actually breaks out on the 17". The Parliament will not be in 
session during those days, because on the 13" the first phase of the session is 
going to be over. 
At least, I do not expect from the most outstanding Parliamentarian 
of this country, when he leads the nation, that on the whole issue, during the 
entire session, the Prime Minister will not speak on the floor of this House or 
the other House on the Iraq situation, a crisis which is evolving in West Asia. 
Thank you for giving me this opportunity.

DR. MANMOHAN SINGH (Assam): Madam, the Budget of the Union 
Government is a major document because it conveys to this House, to this 
Parliament and to the counfry at large, the direction in which the Government 
would like our country to move in the year that lies ahead. 
Madam, Central to wha.t we are planning for the future is a realistic 
appreciation of the current state of the economy. The hon. Finance Minister 
was good enough to present to us a Mid-Year Review of the economy. 
Subsequently, we have the Economic Survey before us. The picture that 
emerges from both these documents in a medium term perspective is that our 
economy is performing far tjelow its potential, and this is more so in the 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2003] 
last four years that the present Government has been in office.   Why do I say 
that? 
Madam, I have looked at the figures of the growth of Gross Domestic 
Product. The average for the last four years is no more than five per cent. 
When it is recalled that when our Government was in office in the mid 90s, the 
national income was growing at a rate exceeding seven per cent per annum, 
the slide-back to the five per cent growth regime should be a matter of 
disappointment for all of us. 
Madam, agriculture in our country accounts for nearly 60 per cent of 
our population and yet, since 1998, the agricultural production has been 
stagnant. The per capita agricultural production in our country after 1998 has, 
in fact, declined.   That is also true of foodgrains production. 
I look at the industrial production. The average rate of growth of 
industrial production in the last four years does not exceed five per cent per 
annum. With regard to imports, the growth rate, in dollar terms, is less than six 
per cent; in exports, it is probably close to 10 per cent. 
Then, Madam, I look at the employment situation. The employment 
data that is given in the Economic Survey reveals that in the organised sector, 
for which reliable figures are available, in the last four years for which figures 
are available - until the year ending March, 2001 - absolute employment has 
been declining in our country since 1998. Now we have a more recent survey 
of the employment situation from the National Sample Survey. It shows an 
alarming situation with regard to the growth of employment in our country. 
Between 1983-84 and 1993-94, the average annual growth of employment 
was about 2.7 per cent. Between 1994 and 2000, it has declined to 1.07 per 
cent. What is more significant is that, in this later period, employment in 
agriculture has been nearly stagnant. 
So, whether we look at the real economy, whether we look at the 
national income, whether we look at agriculture, whether we look at industrial 
production, or whether we look at employment, it is a situation of slide-down all 
along the line. 
Then, what do we find with regard to the fiscal situation? The fiscal 
situation over this period has, also deteriorated.   I look at the figures

[11 March, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
of fiscal deficit. The lowest figure that was reached in 1996-97 was 4.1 per 
cent of GDP and since then, the figure has been going up. The Revised 
Estimates of 2002-03 show near a record figure of 5.9 per cent of the GDP. 
The projected figure for 2003-2004 is 5.6 per cent of GDP. But judging by the 
experience of the last five years, one should, at least, add half-a-per cent more 
to the estimates that are given in the Budget. What is more worrisome, 
Madam, is when the Congress Government was in office, we made a 
determined effort to reduce the revenue deficit. There are differences amongst 
economists in our country and elsewhere on whether we should be worried 
about fiscal deficits or not. But, almost everyone in our cou~htry and abroad is 
agreed that it is not good to have, year after year, revenue deficit to finance 
Government consumption because that is a road to disaster, that is road to 
piling a debt stock which will burden our future generations. Yet we note that in 
the last four years, the revenue deficit has climbed year after year. The 
Revised Estimates of the current year show a revenue deficit of 4.3 of GDP 
per cent, and the hon. Finance Minister has made a marginal token effort to 
reduce it to 4.1 per cent of GDP in the Budget that he has presented for 2003-
2004. 
Madam, I now look at the saving and investment rate in our country. 
The saving and investment rate as well as the public sector saving rate 
reached the peak in the last year of the Congress Government. Since then, 
there has been retrogression or stagnation. Why do I say all this? I am saying 
this not to score a debating point. This country must have a big vision, and I 
support the vision contained in the President's Address that in the next 20 
years, this country must move on to a growth path which will make India a 
front-ranking econQpiy of the world. We and our party will wholeheartedly 
cooperate in genuine efforts that may be made to realise that vision. But, 
Madam, the vision which is not backed by any realistic strategy and 
programme of action merely ends up day-dreaming. 
Madam, the current year happens to be the first year of the Tenth 
Five Year Plan which has an ambitious growth target of eight per cent. This 
country is capable of realising eight per cent growth rate. We, as a nation, 
should commit ourselves to realise that rate. But, the way the economy has 
been sliding down, does not inspire confidence within the country and outside 
the country that this country is moving on to the growth path which we all like 
to achieve in the Tenth Five Year Plan.

per cent in 2001-02. Due to revival in the global prices of steel and increase in 
the local demand because of massive Highway construction programme, the 
cement industry and the steel industry have also revived this year. The steel 
sector grew by 24.5 per cent in the first eight months  of the current fiscal 
year. 
In the case of telecommunications, the new telephone connections 
were up by 17 per cent and the cellular subscriber base has crossed more 
than one crore from just three lakhs, five years ago. The capital goods sector 
which declined by 4.9 per cent during April-November, 2001-02, registered a 
growth of 9.9 per cent in the corresponding period of 2002-03. 
In the case of the textiles sector, which also witnessed a decline in 
2001, showed a short turn around and grew by almost 15 per cent till 
November, 2002, as a result of sharp recovery in the export of readymade 
garments. 
229 

RAJYA SABHA [11 March, 2003] 
In the housing sector, as I mentioned earlier, a lot of activity is going 
on. New areas are coming up and you can see newspapers full of 
advertisements these days asking people to buy houses at a comparatively 
reasonable prices. 
There is no doubt that the economy has acquired new confidence. 
Today, we have foreign exchange reserves of almost 75 billion US dollars. Dr. 
Manmohan Singh is sitting here. He kn ows when he took over, our country 
had foreign exchange reserves just to last two weeks of imports. As I 
mentioned earlier, we had to pawn our gold stocks outside to meet 
international obligations. 
' The profile of our national income is also changing dramatically. The 
GDP at 1993-94 prices, which was Rs. 1,48,000 crores in 1950-51 has grown 
eight times to Rs. 12,66,000 crores in 1999-2000 with annual per capita 
income which grew by three times from Rs. 4,121 to Rs. 12,665. 
Even more dramatic are the changes in the sectoral shares. The 
agriculture sector that contributed 55.4 per cent in 1950-51, now account for 
only 27.5 per cent. While the share of the industrial sector has gone up from 
16.*1 per cent to 24.6 per cent, contribution of the service sector has gone up 
impressively from 28.5 per cent to 47.6 per cent in the same period. But the 
sad fact is, the number of persons employed in the agriculture sector, either as 
cultivators or as labourers, has remained static at almost 70 per cent of the 
total workforce. As I said earlier, no doubt, we are passing through difficult 
times. The country has seen the worst possible droughts for two years in 
succession and the world is at a hand-shaking distance with war in Iraq. 
Needless to say, things can really go bad. As Dr. Manmohan Singh had 
mentioned in his speech, if the war breaks out, the oil prices will go up and 
they are likely to touch 40 dollars per barrel. Of course, we have our Army 
standing at our borders for quite a long time because of tension with Pakistan. 
On the top of it, to add to our problems, there has been a slow down in the 
global economy in the last one year. But even in these difficult circumstances, 
which are beyond the control of this Government, and for that matter beyond 
the control of anybody here, we seem to have done well for ourselves. We 
seem to have done well for ourselves, and in this Budget, Shri Jaswant Singh 
has shown a lot of initiative and imagination. His sector-wise approach, giving 
sector specific thrust,  is noteworthy.     In the matter of textiles,  Madam,  this 
is India's 
230 

[11 March, 2003]                           RAJYA SABHA 
biggest industry in terms of production and employment. The industry will face 
global competition from January 1, 2005, on account of our obligations in the 
World Trade Organisation. Shri Jaswant Singh has taken this problem by the 
horns. He has cut excise duty on polyester, custom duty on textile machinery 
and earmarked huge funds for textile modernisation. This should provide a 
fillip to this industry and hopefully make it more globally competitive. One of 
the major concerns for the small-scale sector industry has the question of 
interest rates. And, the industry has felt that the low-interest-rate scenario has 
remained only on paper. Once again, in an original move, the Finance Minister 
has told the banks that the interest rate chargeable to small-scale industries 
and agriculture would be within the band of 2 per cent or above the prime 
lending rate. 
Madam, I would also like to compliment the Finance Minister for 
making a major beginning in the health sector by according infrastructure 
status to the construction of hospitals with hundred beds and above. By doing 
this, he has opened the doors of financial institutions to private hospitals for 
accessing long-term capital. He has also reduced duties on life-saving drugs 
and equipments, besides widely spreading health insurance net to include the 
poor. Considering that India meets only 40 per cent of W.H.O. defined 
minimum health standards, this thrust is welcome. Similarly, by extending food 
security to more of those living Below the Poverty Line, he has tried to convey 
that economic reforms and poverty alleviation are not mutually exclusive. The 
Budget also provides relief to parents for educating children by extending tax 
concessions. 
Another major thrust has been the renewed emphasis on 
infrastructure. The decision to spend progressively Rs.60,000 crores on 
airports, seaports, roads, etc., should be welcomed by all. And, the way the 
project to link four metros and a highway to connect Kashmir to Kanyakumari 
has taken off, gives us the confidence that it will be possible for the 
Government to build up remarkable infrastructure in the next few years and by 
allotting this sort of amount of Rs.60,000 crores, the Finance Minister has 
shown that commitment. The Budget also restores the faith of senior citizens, 
especially with the introduction of new pension scheme for those above 55 
years. Shri Jaswant Singh's attempt to push private sector banks to open 
branches in rural areas to meet both farm and non-farm credit needs is 
definitely a bold step. 
231 

                       RAJYA SABHA            [11 March, 2003] 
Madam, we are entering a globalised era, the economy is opening up 
and we have to prepare ourselves for international competition. And, I would 
say, Madam, for the first time, a large-scale attempt has been made to reduce 
the cost of production of Indian industry. This is evident from across the board 
cut in excise duties, reduction in peak rates of custom duty, the special 
package for textile, cut in excise duty for automobiles, air-conditioners, are 
some of the steps in the right direction. The Budget will enhance our 
competitive edge, although a large section of the trade continues to be critical 
of introduction of VAT, which is going to be levied from April, 2003. Madam, I 
have seen a lot of criticism by self-proclaimed champions of the farmers over 
the urea prices. In fact, some of them have gone to the extent of calling the 
Budget and the Finance Minister anti-farmer and anti-agriculture because the 
Budget entails an increase of rupees ten per bag in the price of urea. And, I do 
not know whether this hike ia^going. to stay or not. But, it is important to 
understand the logic behind this rise. Over the years, the use of urea has gone 
up due to increased subsidy support, distorting proportionate ratios in the use 
of nitrogenous, phosphoric and potashic fertilizers. And the right ratio is crucial 
for maintaining the soil fertility. The Finance Minister merely tried to rectify this 
distortion in the use of different fertilizers so that soil fertility could be 
preserved. Once this is understood, we will know whether the Finance Minister 
or, to say, the Budget is anti-farmer. Sir, I have also seen some comments 
describing the Budget as soft, ahead of next year's elections. Nothing could 
have been farther from the truth. We have to see the bold initiatives which the 
Finance Minister has taken in this Budget. To name just a few, the cut in small 
savings rate by one per cent, increase in the retention prices of fertilizers and 
acceptance, in principle, of the Kelkar Committee recommendations on direct 
taxes, despite its criticism, are the steps which speak a lot about the FM's 
resolve to put economy back on the rails. This apart, the import duty on gold 
has been cut from Rs.250 per 10 gms. to Rs.100, and the Finance Minister has 
talked of his ambition to make India a major international gold trading centre. 
What a change from the time, just a few years back, when gold import was not 
allowed, and smugglers were laughing all the way to their banks! In fact, for 40 
years, even people with white incomes could not buy the white gold for the 
simple reason that India did not produce gold. It did not import gold; it only 
consumed gold. The consumption was so much, that is about 500 tonnes a 
year, and the solitary gold mine of Kolar used to produce less than half a tonne. 
The rest of the gold was all smuggled into the country and smugglers made a 
killing, and even honest 
232 

[11 March, 2003]                            RAJYA SABHA 
people were forced to buy gold from the black market and without a proper 
receipt. Fortunately, things are changing. The Government is making revenue 
and people are able to meet their legitimate demand for gold through 
legitimate sources. 
Madam, Dr. Manmohan Singh expressed a lot of concerns over the 
inflation rate. These concerns are justifiable enough because normally a high 
inflation rate cuts into the savings of the poor, and it affects the poor much 
more than the rich. But I would like to compliment the Finance Minister for 
keeping the inflation under check. As it is, the 12-month rise in wholesale price 
index has gone up from just 1.2 per cent in February, 2002, to over 5 per cent 
a year later. I have been looking at the composition of the change in the index 
and it is clear that the rise has been fuelled much more by primary goods - no 
surprise in a year of drought - and fuel prices. Manufacturing inflation has also 
gone up, but nowhere nearby as large a percentage as in the other two 
segments. One expects that the prices of oil and, therefore, fuel, will come 
down once the confrontation in Iraq gets over; in any case, we can do very 
little about it. As for agriculture output, the last decade's history shows that the 
output in the segment of the economy has gone up and down in alternate 
years. If the pattern holds, 2003-04 should witness a significant rise in output; 
in any case, there are enough buffer stocks to control the price rises. Madam, 
the Finance Minister has also shown the way to put the economy's huge 
foreign exchange pile, at 75 billion dollars, to good use. Now, the corporates 
can repay external commercial borrowings up to 100 million US dollars 
automatically. Further, he has announced that the sector will continue pre-
payment of high cost World Bank and Asian Development Bank loans. 
Madam, three billion US Dollars has already been paid in the current year. 
Using idle capital for repaying high-cost loans is surely a prudent decision. I 
compliment him for this imaginative measure. Madam, ours is a federal 
structure. If States' health is poor, the country cannot be healthy. Jaswant 
Singhji has taken note of this reality. The beleaguered States, with their 
mounting debt burden, may receive some comfort from the Budget. Madam, 
the States owe Rs.2.44,000 crores to the Government of India, out of this a 
little over Rs. one lakh crore bear coupon rates upwards of 13 per cent per 
annum, much in excess of the current market rates. As a result, the interest 
burden of the States now comprises a major item of expenditure for them, 
leaving little leeway for even managing their essential expenditures. It is, in the 
light of this situation that the Central and the State Governments 
233 

                           RAJYA SABHA              [11 March, 2003] 
have mutually agreed to introduce a debt-swap scheme, the aim of which is to 
utilise the current low interest rate regime to enable the States pre-pay 
expensive loans contracted from the Centre in the past, with the current low 
coupon bearing small savings and open market loans. Even, as efforts go on 
towards translating the debt-swap scheme into reality by working out the 
modalities, the Budget proposal to bring into vogue the Value Added Tax 
(VAT) is surely a historic reform of the outdated domestic trade tax system. 
Besides eliminating cascading of taxes, the advent of VAT is likely to increase 
revenue as the coverage widens to include value addition at all stages of sale. 
Madam, despite the initiatives to push up the financial position of States, 
ultimately it is the States that have to help themselves. Unfortunately, the 
situation as it exists now, in this regard, to State finances can only be termed 
as ^dismal. A worrisome feature of the expenditure patterns of the States is 
that the growth rate in development expenditure at 4.1 per cent in 2002-03 will 
be far lower than the growth rate of 11.7 per cent in non-developmental 
expenditure. What is disturbing is that, under non-developmental expenditure, 
the major items; of interest payments, expenditure on administrative services 
and pensioners are budgeted to account for 30.8 per cent of the total 
expenditure and absorb 43.3 per cent of the total revenue receipts c* the 
States in 2002-03. While the revenue deficit of all States taken together is 
estimated to account for 47 per cent of gross fiscal deficit, the State-wise 
position indicates that revenue deficit will account for more than 60 per cent of 
the GFD in the case of Kerala, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Gujarat, 
Rajasthan and Maharashtra. A glance at States' debt and guarantees will be 
an eye opener as to how almost all the States have been living beyond their 
means. At the end of March, 2002, the combined outstanding debt of States 
amounted to Rs.5,89,000 crores. Between the end of March, 2001 and the 
end of March, 2002, the States' debt rose by 18.3 per cent. As a percentage of 
GDP, the debt stock of States rose to 25.7 per cent at the end of March, 2002 
from 23.7 per cent earlier. Yet another disturbing trend in the finances is that 
outstanding guarantees provided by the States for projects put up in the States 
have increased from Rs.42,515 crores at the end of March, 1993 to a 
staggering figure of Rs.1,66.116 crores at the end of March, 2002, for as many 
as seventeen major States. Finally, a neglected area, where State 
Governments could take initiative to improve .the policy environment of 
investment, relates to the degree of flexibility allowed with regard to the labogr 
laws. It is commonly said that our labour laws are too inflexible. The need to 
amend the Central legislation to allow flexibility has been 
234 

[11 March, 2003]                            RAJYA SABHA 
pointed out on many occasions. The State Governments could formulate more 
flexible guidelines within which the State Governments would act on these 
matters. Madam, the State Governments must .make a serious effort to get 
out of the public sector enterprises. Many of the State PSUs are-nothing but 
little more than vehicles for creating jobs at all levels. In many-States, political 
personalities are appointed as Chairmen of State Corporations and given the 
rank of Cabinet Ministers. More and more State PSUs are unlikely to yield 
significant resources if privatised, though privatisation could avoid recurring 
losses. However, there are some that could be privatised with an immediate 
budgetary gain. The various tourism corporations, or public sector sugar mills, 
or cement plants owned by so many State Governments, are examples of 
units where a start can be made.

total expenditure of Rs. 1.27 crores, were sanctioned. The Bannalal 
Committee's investigations disclosed that only 21 works were found on the 
sites...

continue to suffer, if this is all the Finance Minister has got to offer. 
I would like to see how the real interest rates came down. The real 
credit to agriculturists is provided by the cooperative sector. Now, there is 
nothing on cooperative banking reforms. We had a huge scam in the 
cooperative sector. What has been done in that regard? Has any culprit been 
punished? Has the issue of dual control system of cooperative banks been 
addressed?  No, Sir.   That has not been addressed. 
Sir, the VAT regime is a welcome initiative. It had been conceived 
many years back. We are making a slow progress. Now, the Finance Minister 
has announced that we will move to a completely new VAT regime by 1s' April, 
2003. But, are the States ready? A private survey published in this morning's 
newspapers indicates that none of the States is ready. This is a very complex 
regime. You do not have even the legislation in place yet. We need to go to 
VAT; there is no doubt about that. But the preparations are not there. Australia 
adopted the Value-Added Tax Regime. They went through a complete public 
education and advertising campaign for one whole year. People were told 
what to do. A complete dry-run was there for one whole year. The whole 
country was splashed with advertisements regarding what this new rggime 
was all about. We have not done anything of that sort. I am sure,.when we go 
to the new tax regime, there will be problems, and the industry will suffer 
because the Government is not clear. I wish the Finance Minister brought out 
a White Paper, and what did he want to do; how does he want to go about; 
what is the road map in the next year for moving to the VAT regime. The 
Finance Minister has also promised us a service-tax legislation. Why could we 
not come out with the proposal right now?   How long will we have to wait for 
the new 
266 

[11 March, 2003]  RAJYA SABHA 
legislation in respect of service-tax to come about? The service-tax had been 
introduced long time back. But there is still no comprehensive legislation. 
There is only a talk. There is only a promise. Sir, talking of promises, there are 
many more promises in the Budget Speech. We have been talking, for a long 
time, about the Limited Partnership Act. Why are there promises only? Why 
don't you do something about it? The previous Finance Minister had talked 
about labour law reforms. People are worried; the labour class is worried 
about what you want to do about it. Will he clarify as to what the Government 
wants to do? Will he build a consensus within his party, and then come to us 
to indicate what he wants to do? He has talked about service law legislation 
also. Again, it is a promise; but nothing has been done. Then he has 
announced task forces -- task force to study drip irrigation, task force to study 
the feasibility and priority of interlinking the rivers. But no money has been 
sanctioned for interlinking the rivers. 
Now, I come to infrastructure sector. Again, the Finance Minister has 
thrown a very big figure - Rs. 60,000 crores worth of infrastructure schemes. 
Fine! He has talked about five infrastructure schemes. But how much money 
has he allotted for these schemes? Only Rs. 2000 crores! From where the 
rest, Rs. 58000 crores, is going to come? From public-private partnership! A 
new phrase! But aren't all projects public-private partnership projects? Take, 
for example, the Dabhol project. Was it entirely financed by the private sector? 
No. The private sector brought in some money, but it was financed by the 
public sector banks, the public sector financial institutions and so on. So, what 
is the new innovation? What is the new thing that he is going to leverage Rs. 
2000 crores into projects worth Rs.60,000 crores. Great! If this is the leverage 
ratio, can an interlinking project worth Rs. 6 lakh crores be completed with 
Rs.20,000 crores of the Government's money? Even that has not been 
provided for. I think, this is a wishful thinking, just a new nomenclature. I don't 
think this will really get us anywhere. Sir, there are many areas of which we 
are worried about. But, before I conclude, I wish to bring to the notice of this 
House is the opportunity that has been lost. The Kelkar task force had offered 
a road map for a simple, predictable and stable long-term tax regime which 
would have freed an honest tax payer from the clutches of the dishonest tax 
inspector. But the present regime is riddled with exemptions, exceptions, 
notifications, schedules and lists, there were over thousands of notifications, 
issued last year, modifying the customs and excise tarrifs.   This 
267 

RAJYA SABHA   [11 March, 2003] 
gives discretionary power to the inspector; this gives an advantage to the 
dishonest taxpayer who in collusion with the dishonest tax inspector gets a 
break, and the honest taxpayers suffer. This is because he does not have an 
expensive tax lawyer; he does not have expensive tax consultants. We had 
got the opportunity to simplify the regime, but the political pressure, a few 
vested interests sabotaged the whole report. Only certain parts were accepted 
which the industrial sector wanted, but the broad reform in the tax system was 
not done. A great opportunity has been lost. We are, again, a prisoner of a 
system consisting of discretionary exemption raj. And, he has further 
complicated that discretionary exemption raj, by tinkering with the tax rates, 
and, has only reinforced that kind of regime. Sir, I wish the hon. Finance 
Minister had not given the tax sop to the rich. He has foregone the tax revenue 
to the tune of more than Rs.3,000 crores from the rich, in the form of direct 
taxes. This money could have been very well utilised in increasing the public 
expenditure on agriculture, increasing the public expenditure, which was badly 
required, in creating new jobs, but he has not done that. Again, without this 
public spending, there will be no demand push. There will be no demand for 
the products which the industries want to create and the industries will 
continue to stagnate. Perhaps, his political mandate, in the year when we are 
going to have State Assembly elections, was to please the rich, the upper 
middle class, the urban voters.the stock market operators, corporate board 
rooms, the readers of pink economic papers and viewers of cable TV, the 
people who advertise on those cable TV channel, the vocal minority which, 
apparently, do not mould the public opinion much. The entire objective was to 
create a feel-good effect so that benefits will come in the forthcoming 
elections. But the people will not be fooled by these gimmicks because, unless 
economy really grows, unless jobs are created, unless farmers' miseries are 
mitigated, the Government will not get the quick benefit of winning the 
elections. Sir, I conclude by saying that a great opportunity to reform the 
system, to achieve a growth rate of 8 per cent or 9 per cent has been lost.   
Thank you.
